newsitem.title: USA: Oil and grain prices fall as supply concerns fade.
newsitem.headline: Oil and grain prices fall as supply concerns fade.

text.p: Oil and grain prices fell Friday as concerns about short supplies eased.
Heating oil prices ended lower after oil inventory data showed supplies grew significantly amid weak demand.

Late Thursday, the American Petroleum Institute said in its weekly report that U.S. stockpiles of distillate, or diesel and heating oil, grew 2.47 million barrels for the week ended Dec. 27. This compared with expectations of a rise of less than one million barrels.
Also, distillate demand dropped to 3.39 million barrels a day from 4.12 million a week earlier while distillate production stood at 3.49 million bpd in the latest week.

"The stock numbers certainly are not supportive, and it seems the supply/demand picture for heat has really deteriorated," said Bob MacMinn, president of petroleum consulting firm MPAS Inc. in Toronto.

On the New York Mercantile Exchange, heating oil for February delivery settled 0.82 cent lower at 71.29 cents a gallon. Dealers said the drop would have been steeper had it not been for the relative strength of February crude oil, which closed 10 cents a barrel lower at $25.59.
February gasoline fell in line with heating oil's weakness, ending off 0.40 cent at 70.70 cents a gallon.
Energy traders also noted that the most recent six- to 10-day forecast from the National Weather Service called for above normal temperatures in the U.S. Northeast.
As of Dec 27, U.S. distillate stocks were only 5.4 million barrels below last year's levels -- down from a 19.8 million barrel deficit in August.
"Distillate stocks are only 5.4 million barrels below a year ago now, so barring any real prolonged cold spell, it looks bearish," said Victor Yu, vice president of brokers Refco in New York.
Lack of export demand keyed selling of grain contracts at the Chicago Board of Trade on Friday.
March corn fell 2 cents a bushel to close at $2.56-1/2, March wheat fell 5-1/4 cents a bushel at $3.84, and January soybeans fell 3 cents a bushel at $6.96-1/4.

Traders sold wheat contracts after Sri Lanka bought 100,000 metric tons of Australian and Argentine wheat, avoiding the higher priced U.S. market. News that Egypt would also not buy over the weekend pressured prices.

Corn and soybeans were pressured by lower-than-expected weekly export sales, with corn sales of 447,000 tons below trade expectations of 450,000 to 600,000 tons and soybean sales of 293,100 tons much lower than expectations for 400,000 to 500,000 tons, floor traders said.

Traders also cited a private estimate by influential crop consultant Sparks Companies of Memphis that put the final 1996 U.S. corn crop at 9.295 billion bushels and soybean crop at 2.403 billion bushels, both upward revisions for the harvest completed last month.
